entities.name: Battle of Thymbra
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Battle of Thymbra was a pivotal conflict between the Lydian Empire under Croesus and the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great, fought on May 5, 546 BCE, near modern-day Bergama, Turkey. This epic clash of ancient powers had far-reaching consequences for the region and the wider world, as the Achaemenid Empire emerged victorious, absorbing Lydia and expanding its dominion over the ancient Near East.

The battle was a decisive turning point in the Lydian-Achaemenid Wars, marking the end of Lydian independence and the beginning of Achaemenid rule in the region. The Achaemenid Empire, under Cyrus the Great, would go on to become one of the largest empires of the ancient world, stretching from modern-day Iran and parts of Turkey to Egypt and the Persian Gulf.

The significance of the Battle of Thymbra extends beyond the confines of ancient history, as it highlights the complexities of cultural exchange and conflict in the ancient world. The clash of civilizations between the Lydians and the Achaemenids serves as a reminder of the enduring impact of historical events on the development of human societies.

In the words of the ancient Greek historian Herodotus, 'The Lydians were the first people to use gold coins, and the Lydians were the first people to use gold coins in a way that was unknown to the Greeks.' This quote highlights the cultural significance of the Battle of Thymbra, as it underscores the Lydians' innovative use of gold currency, which would have far-reaching consequences for the development of commerce and trade in the ancient world.
